evidence.claim: The President holds executive power, may submit bills, issue implementing regulations, and is assisted by a Vice-President and ministers whom the President appoints and dismisses.
evidence.title: Indonesia 1945 (reinst. 1959, rev. 2002) Constitution
evidence.excerpt: The President holds executive power, may submit bills, issue implementing regulations, and is assisted by a Vice-President and ministers whom the President appoints and dismisses.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Constitutional text directly states executive authority and cabinet appointment/removal powers.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Direct institutional authority; these powers belong to the Indonesian presidency, not to Jokowi personally alone.
contrary_evidence: Legislative bargaining and coalition politics can constrain how much of this authority is usable in practice.

evidence.claim: The World Bank approved a $750 million loan to help Indonesia increase tax revenue, improve tax system equity, and strengthen institutions for more efficient planning and spending.
evidence.title: New Support Will Help Strengthen Indonesia’s Tax System, Improve Development Spending
evidence.excerpt: The World Bank approved a $750 million loan to help Indonesia increase tax revenue, improve tax system equity, and strengthen institutions for more efficient planning and spending.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Official World Bank press release with dated, specific policy measures and financing terms.
evidence.period_fit: Directly covers 2022 fiscal-policy priorities and implementation support.
evidence.ruler_attribution: High for national fiscal policy direction under Jokowi; implementation also depended on the finance ministry and legislative/legal follow-through.
contrary_evidence: This is financing support, not proof that all reforms worked fully in 2022.
The press release also notes low revenue intake and shallow financial markets, which limited the baseline.

evidence.claim: Sri Mulyani said the Harmonized Taxation Law was a milestone of Indonesia’s tax reforms, aiming to improve growth, optimize state revenue, realize fair taxation, provide legal certainty, reform administration, broaden the tax base, and introduce 2022 VAT and income-tax changes.
evidence.title: Gov’t to Optimize Fair State Revenue through Harmonized Taxation Law, Minister Says
evidence.excerpt: Sri Mulyani said the Harmonized Taxation Law was a milestone of Indonesia’s tax reforms, aiming to improve growth, optimize state revenue, realize fair taxation, provide legal certainty, reform administration, broaden the tax base, and introduce 2022 VAT and income-tax changes.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Official cabinet-secretariat transcription of the finance minister’s policy explanation with concrete tax measures and implementation dates.
evidence.period_fit: Pre-2022 enactment that directly shaped 2022 tax policy and implementation.
evidence.ruler_attribution: High for policy direction because the law was government policy under Jokowi’s administration, though ministerial leadership was central.
contrary_evidence: The item states intent and design, not final economic outcomes.
It reflects ministerial explanation rather than an independent audit of implementation quality.

evidence.claim: The finance minister said the 2022 voluntary disclosure program gave taxpayers until June 30, 2022 to disclose unmet obligations voluntarily and improve compliance, with special treatment for previously undeclared assets and a small revenue yield by early February.
evidence.title: Menkeu Ajak Wajib Pajak Manfaatkan Program Pengungkapan Sukarela
evidence.excerpt: The finance minister said the 2022 voluntary disclosure program gave taxpayers until June 30, 2022 to disclose unmet obligations voluntarily and improve compliance, with special treatment for previously undeclared assets and a small revenue yield by early February.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Official government announcement with specific dates, rates, and early participation figures.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Medium-high for tax administration under Jokowi; the initiative is minister-led but part of the national economic policy line.
contrary_evidence: A voluntary program does not prove broad fairness or full compliance.
Early participation and receipts are positive but limited evidence of long-run structural improvement.

evidence.claim: Jokowi said the BBM subsidy budget had tripled to Rp502.4 trillion, that more than 70 percent benefited wealthier car owners, and that the government would shift part of the subsidy into targeted cash transfers and wage support for poorer households and workers.
evidence.title: Penyataan Pers Presiden RI mengenai Pengalihan Subsidi BBM
evidence.excerpt: Jokowi said the BBM subsidy budget had tripled to Rp502.4 trillion, that more than 70 percent benefited wealthier car owners, and that the government would shift part of the subsidy into targeted cash transfers and wage support for poorer households and workers.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Direct presidential transcript with concrete fiscal numbers, targeting logic, and named transfer programs.
evidence.period_fit: Directly covers a major 2022 policy choice made in response to the fuel-price shock.
evidence.ruler_attribution: High; this was a presidential decision and public justification, though execution was shared with ministries and local governments.
contrary_evidence: This is self-justifying executive rhetoric, though the quoted figures are concrete and testable.
The policy was a response to a shock, not proof of broader structural prosperity.

evidence.claim: PMK 134/PMK.07/2022 required local governments to budget social-protection spending for October-December 2022, including support for ojek, UMKM, fishers, and transport subsidies, funded at least at 2 percent of the general transfer base.
evidence.title: 134/PMK.07/2022 - Belanja Wajib dalam rangka Penanganan Dampak Inflasi Tahun Anggaran 2022
evidence.excerpt: PMK 134/PMK.07/2022 required local governments to budget social-protection spending for October-December 2022, including support for ojek, UMKM, fishers, and transport subsidies, funded at least at 2 percent of the general transfer base.
evidence.source_locator: summary bullets on social-protection budgeting and permissible uses
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Official legal summary with concrete spending rules and implementation requirements.
evidence.period_fit: Directly covers a 2022 inflation-response spending rule.
evidence.ruler_attribution: High for national fiscal design; the rule was issued by the finance ministry under Jokowi’s administration, though subnational execution varied.
contrary_evidence: This sets a rule; it does not by itself prove local compliance or household outcomes.
A mandated floor may still be too blunt or unevenly targeted in practice.

evidence.claim: The IMF said Indonesia’s authorities had responded with a bold, comprehensive, well-coordinated policy package that maintained economic and financial stability, and it welcomed gradual withdrawal of extraordinary support, a return to the fiscal rule, and using subsidy savings to strengthen the social safety net.
evidence.title: IMF Executive Board Concludes 2022 Article IV Consultation with Indonesia
evidence.excerpt: The IMF said Indonesia’s authorities had responded with a bold, comprehensive, well-coordinated policy package that maintained economic and financial stability, and it welcomed gradual withdrawal of extraordinary support, a return to the fiscal rule, and using subsidy savings to strengthen the social safety net.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Official IMF surveillance summary with explicit policy assessment and recommendations.
evidence.period_fit: Directly covers Indonesia’s 2022 macro-policy environment and the inherited recovery phase.
evidence.ruler_attribution: High for fiscal and macro-policy choices under Jokowi, but not exclusive credit because BI, accumulated buffers, and global conditions mattered.
contrary_evidence: The IMF also says the outlook remained tilted to the downside and recovery benefited from accumulated policy buffers.
Some positive outcomes were not uniquely Jokowi’s; they also reflected pre-existing buffers and external conditions.

evidence.claim: Bank Indonesia reported that 2022 CPI inflation ended at 5.51 percent after subsidized fuel prices were adjusted in September 2022, and said lower inflation reflected close coordination between the government and BI through a front-loaded, pre-emptive response and food-inflation control measures.
evidence.title: Monetary Policy Report - Quarter IV 2022
evidence.excerpt: Bank Indonesia reported that 2022 CPI inflation ended at 5.51 percent after subsidized fuel prices were adjusted in September 2022, and said lower inflation reflected close coordination between the government and BI through a front-loaded, pre-emptive response and food-inflation control measures.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Official central-bank report with specific inflation figures and policy attribution.
evidence.period_fit: Directly reports end-2022 inflation outcomes and the policy response taken during 2022.
evidence.ruler_attribution: High for the fuel-price decision and fiscal coordination; medium for inflation outcomes because BI policy was independent and global price pressures were material.
contrary_evidence: Inflation still exceeded the target band, so the stabilization was partial rather than complete.
The report credits both government and Bank Indonesia, not Jokowi alone.

evidence.claim: The World Bank projected 5.2 percent growth in 2022, said Indonesia’s conditions remained stable amid global shocks, and noted that growth was boosted by reopening and commodity prices while fiscal consolidation was helped by high commodity revenues and lower COVID-related spending.
evidence.title: Indonesia’s Economy Sees Rebound in 2022 following Post-Covid Reopening
evidence.excerpt: The World Bank projected 5.2 percent growth in 2022, said Indonesia’s conditions remained stable amid global shocks, and noted that growth was boosted by reopening and commodity prices while fiscal consolidation was helped by high commodity revenues and lower COVID-related spending.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Official World Bank press release with concrete macroeconomic assessment and explicit attribution caveats.
evidence.period_fit: Directly covers the 2022 economy and near-end-2022 fiscal conditions.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Moderate: the outcome reflects Jokowi-era policy, but the source explicitly credits reopening and commodity prices as major drivers.
contrary_evidence: The same source attributes much of the rebound to reopening and commodity prices, limiting direct ruler credit.
It also says downside risks remained significant.

evidence.claim: By 14 December 2022, Indonesia’s tax revenue had reached 110.06 percent of target and grown 41.93 percent year on year, with the finance minister attributing the result to good economic growth, recovery, higher commodity prices, and tax-law reform.
evidence.title: Tax Revenue Reaches 110.06 Percent
evidence.excerpt: By 14 December 2022, Indonesia’s tax revenue had reached 110.06 percent of target and grown 41.93 percent year on year, with the finance minister attributing the result to good economic growth, recovery, higher commodity prices, and tax-law reform.
evidence.source_locator: opening paragraphs of the press item
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Official government press item with a concrete year-end fiscal result and attribution statement, though it is a ministerial readout rather than an audit.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Medium-high for fiscal-policy success; the result is partly policy-driven but also partly windfall-driven.
contrary_evidence: The stated drivers include commodity prices and broad recovery, so the result is not purely a Jokowi-policy effect.
A press item is not a full independent audit of revenue quality or sustainability.

evidence.claim: BPS reported that Indonesia’s 2022 economy grew 5.31 percent, with GDP per capita of Rp71.0 million or US$4,783.9, and that transportation/storage and exports were the leading growth components.
evidence.title: Ekonomi Indonesia Tahun 2022 Tumbuh 5,31 Persen
evidence.excerpt: BPS reported that Indonesia’s 2022 economy grew 5.31 percent, with GDP per capita of Rp71.0 million or US$4,783.9, and that transportation/storage and exports were the leading growth components.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Official national statistics release with clear 2022 macro indicators.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Low-to-moderate because this is an aggregate national outcome affected by reopening, commodities, and external demand as well as policy.
contrary_evidence: The statistic itself does not isolate Jokowi’s contribution.
The growth mix was heavily influenced by sectors and external conditions beyond the presidency.

evidence.claim: BPS reported that the August 2022 open unemployment rate was 5.86 percent, down 0.63 points from August 2021, while average labor wages were Rp3.07 million per month and employment increased by 4.25 million people year on year.
evidence.title: Agustus 2022: Tingkat Pengangguran Terbuka (TPT) sebesar 5,86 persen dan Rata-rata upah buruh sebesar 3,07 juta rupiah per bulan
evidence.excerpt: BPS reported that the August 2022 open unemployment rate was 5.86 percent, down 0.63 points from August 2021, while average labor wages were Rp3.07 million per month and employment increased by 4.25 million people year on year.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Official labor-force survey release with direct 2022 labor-market figures.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Low-to-moderate because this is an economy-wide outcome shaped by recovery, not a ruler-only decision.
contrary_evidence: The release is a snapshot, not a causal policy audit.
It still shows underemployment and pandemic scarring, so household security was improving but not solved.

evidence.claim: BPS reported that the poverty rate in September 2022 was 9.57 percent, or 26.36 million people, slightly higher than March 2022 but lower than September 2021.
evidence.title: Persentase Penduduk Miskin September 2022 naik menjadi 9,57 persen
evidence.excerpt: BPS reported that the poverty rate in September 2022 was 9.57 percent, or 26.36 million people, slightly higher than March 2022 but lower than September 2021.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Official statistics release with direct poverty data and comparison points.
evidence.period_fit: Directly reports a target-year household welfare outcome as of September 2022.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Low-to-moderate because poverty is an aggregate outcome influenced by many factors, though policy responses to inflation and transfers matter.
contrary_evidence: Poverty rose slightly from March 2022, so the household picture was not uniformly improving.
The measure reflects broad conditions, not Jokowi’s actions alone.

evidence.claim: BPS reported that Indonesia’s September 2022 Gini ratio was 0.381, down from 0.384 in March 2022 and unchanged from September 2021.
evidence.title: Gini Ratio September 2022 tercatat sebesar 0,381
evidence.excerpt: BPS reported that Indonesia’s September 2022 Gini ratio was 0.381, down from 0.384 in March 2022 and unchanged from September 2021.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Official inequality statistics release with explicit comparison points.
evidence.period_fit: Directly reports a target-year distributional outcome.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Low-to-moderate because inequality is shaped by many structural factors, though transfer policy and inflation response can affect it.
contrary_evidence: The change was small, so the distributional improvement was modest.
The measure does not isolate any single policy, leader, or region.

evidence.claim: Transparency International reported Indonesia’s 2022 CPI score at 34 out of 100, rank 110 of 180, down 4 points from 2021, indicating continued weak anti-corruption performance.
evidence.title: Corruption Perceptions Index 2022
evidence.excerpt: Transparency International reported Indonesia’s 2022 CPI score at 34 out of 100, rank 110 of 180, down 4 points from 2021, indicating continued weak anti-corruption performance.
evidence.source_locator: country page and global-results text for Indonesia
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Well-known cross-country corruption index with a clear 2022 country score, though perception-based rather than direct observation.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Medium: the score reflects the broader governing environment under Jokowi, but it is not a ruler-specific audit and is perception-based.
contrary_evidence: The CPI is a perception index, not a direct measure of a single leader’s actions.
It does not distinguish inherited problems from Jokowi-era choices.

evidence.claim: Jokowi inaugurated two ministers and three vice ministers on June 15, 2022 for the remainder of the 2019-2024 term, under presidential decrees dismissing and appointing ministers and vice ministers.
evidence.title: President Jokowi Reshuffles Indonesia Onward Cabinet
evidence.excerpt: Jokowi inaugurated two ministers and three vice ministers on June 15, 2022 for the remainder of the 2019-2024 term, under presidential decrees dismissing and appointing ministers and vice ministers.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Official cabinet-secretariat record of actual ministerial appointments and presidential decrees.
evidence.period_fit: Directly covers a 2022 cabinet appointment event.
evidence.ruler_attribution: High for appointment authority and cabinet composition; it does not itself show whether the appointees were economically optimal.
contrary_evidence: This proves appointment power, not economic competence.
Two of the new appointees were not clearly economic technocrats, so the item is only partial evidence for 5B.2.

evidence.claim: The Jakarta Post reported that the trade minister was replaced after soaring cooking-oil prices and nationwide shortages, and that Zulkifli Hasan’s appointment continued a revolving-door pattern in the trade portfolio.
evidence.title: Jokowi orders seventh Cabinet reshuffle
evidence.excerpt: The Jakarta Post reported that the trade minister was replaced after soaring cooking-oil prices and nationwide shortages, and that Zulkifli Hasan’s appointment continued a revolving-door pattern in the trade portfolio.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Reputable newspaper reporting on a concrete cabinet change, but with some interpretive framing.
evidence.period_fit: Directly covers the June 2022 cabinet reshuffle during the target year.
evidence.ruler_attribution: High for Jokowi’s choice of appointees and response to the cooking-oil crisis; the underlying price shock was broader than the presidency.
contrary_evidence: The article is journalistic interpretation rather than a formal economic audit.
The reshuffle can be read as crisis response rather than proof of long-term technocratic selection.
